Genetic correlation between fat mass percentage and cardiorespiratory capacity suggest a shared genetic basis for both traits.

we observed that body fat percentage (BF%) and cardiorespiratory capacity (CRF) are genetically correlated (ρG =-0.72, p = 2.3×10-6), and that a genetic risk score based on 12 known BF% increasing loci associates with CRF (β = - 0.15 mL O2/kg/min per allele p = 0,0034, age, sex and body fat percentage adjusted).
The genetic correlation between body fat percentage and cardiorespiratoryfitness was -0.72, indicating a common genetic origin of these traits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between body fat and cardiorespiratory function, which are important factors in determining health and disease.
genetic factors that affect the body fat% and cardiorespiratory function.
the relationship between body fat and cardiorespiratory (CR) fitness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a genetic risk score for body fat% associates with CRF, but that this association is mediated through the fat mass and that it is not due to fat-free mass.
the same genes that increase fat mass also increase fat free mass, and the genes that increase both fat and fat free mass also decrease VO2max.

the genetic factors that influence fat mass also have a negative impact on fitness, and that the genetic factors influencing body fat% are not specific to the fat mass but also influence other body compartments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
genetic variants associated with higher body fat% also associate with lower CRF, and that the FTO locus is a major determinant of both traits.
a genetic propensity to accumulate fat is associated with a lower VO2max.

the body fat%-increased FTO risk allele and the body fat%-related genetic risk variants are associated with lower CRF, but this association is explained by the body fat%-associated genetic variants and body fat% itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic risk variants for increased body fat% also associate with lower levels of fitness.
the genetic factors that promote whole body fat% are also related to CRF, and vice versa.
a genetic risk score for body fat% can be used to predict CRF, and thus, a genetic risk score could be a useful predictor of health status.
